{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Ernst Constantin Fetterlein''' (3 April 1873<ref name=madeira>Victor Madeira, "`Because I Don't Trust Him, We are Friends': Signals Intelligence and the Reluctant Anglo-Soviet Embrace, 1917-24", ''Intelligence & National Security'' 19(1), March 2004, pp. 29&ndash;51.</ref> – June 1944<ref name=freebmd>{{Cite web|url=https://www.freebmd.org.uk/cgi/information.pl?cite=HAEnScTI2gKOy9JjBNhQYA&scan=1|title=Index entry|accessdate=19 September 2022|work=FreeBMD|publisher=ONS}}</ref><ref name=erskine>Ralph Erskine, [http://archives.his.com/intelforum/2004-October/msg00055.html Internet post] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060507085221/http://archives.his.com/intelforum/2004-October/msg00055.html |date=2006-05-07 }} to [[Intelligence Forum]], 11 October 2004</ref>) was a [[Russian (citizen)|Russian]] [[cryptographer]] who later defected to [[United Kingdom|Britain]].

Fetterlein was born in [[St Petersburg]], the son of Karl Fedorovich Fetterlein, a German-language tutor, and Olga Fetterlein, née Meier.<ref name="madeira"/> He studied a variety of eastern languages at the [[University of St Petersburg]], graduating in 1894. On 25 November 1896 he joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.<ref name="madeira"/> He eventually became the chief cryptologist for the [[Tsar of Russia]],<ref name="bud56">Stephen Budiansky, ''Battle of Wits'', 2000, {{ISBN|0-670-88492-8}}, p. 56</ref> holding the rank of "General-Admiral," an honorary title in Tsarist Russia.<ref name="smith">Michael Smith, "GC&CS and the First Cold War", pp. 1-40 in ''Action This Day'', 2001, {{ISBN|0-593-04982-9}}</ref> During [[World War I]], he was known for a time as '''Ernst Popov''' as his German-derived name could have drawn unwanted attention.<ref>Thomas R Hammant, "Russian and Soviet cryptology: II &mdash; the Magdeburg incident: The Russian view", in ''Cryptologia'', October 2000</ref> Amongst others, he solved German, Austrian and British codes.<ref name=smith/>

Upon the [[Russian Revolution of 1917]], he fled to Western Europe with his wife on board a Swedish ship, narrowly evading capture.<ref name=smith/> He contacted the British and French intelligence organisations, offering to work for whoever would pay him the most, which was apparently the British, as he was recruited to [[Room 40]] in June 1918<ref name=smith/> to work on [[Democratic Republic of Georgia|Georgian]], Austrian and Bolshevik codes. After the end of World War I, he worked for the successor to Room 40, the [[Government Code and Cypher School]] (GC&CS), becoming a senior assistant on 17 December 1919.<ref name=madeira/> During this time he worked on Soviet Communist traffic.<ref>[[David Kahn (writer)|David Kahn]], ''Seizing the Enigma'', 1991, {{ISBN|0-09-978411-4}}, p. 85</ref> He was thought well of by his colleagues, one of whom wrote, "He was a brilliant cryptographer. On book cipher and anything else where insight was vital he was quite the best. He was a fine linguist and would usually get an answer no matter the language."<ref name=smith/> He retired in 1938.<ref name=erskine/> His brother, P. K. Fetterlein, also worked for GC&CS.<ref name=smith/>

Fetterlein came out of retirement during [[World War II]] to assist GC&CS's diplomatic section at Berkeley Street. He worked on "[[Floradora]]", a German diplomatic code.<ref>Budiansky, 2000, p. 219</ref>
